title: Two Moments, Two Models
hook: Spotting unhappy delivery customers from a six-question survey by pairing two models that each read a different moment of the journey

slides.title: Two Moments, Two Models
slides.subtitle: Customer happiness prediction for a logistics and delivery startup
slides.narration: A fast-growing delivery startup wanted to know which customers are unhappy before they leave. Divyesh found that happiness depends on two different moments, and built a model for each.

slides.title: The problem
bullets: A customer survey with six statements, each rated 1 to 5: on-time delivery, contents as expected, ordered everything wanted, good price, courier, and app
Target: is the customer happy or unhappy?
Main goal: catch as many unhappy customers as possible (unhappy recall)
Constraint: still recognise at least 64% of happy customers
slides.narration: The aim was to catch unhappy customers early, without wrongly flagging lots of happy ones along the way.

slides.title: The data at a glance
bullets: A very small dataset, so every result needs careful checking
50-fold repeated stratified cross-validation on the training set
slides.narration: Only 126 responses, which is tiny. That shaped every decision: with this little data, it's easy to fool yourself, so he checked results with cross-validation too.

slides.title: Which questions carry signal?
slides.unit: Votes from three independent checks (point-biserial correlation, chi-square, Random Forest importance)
bullets: Price and app got no votes from any check, so they were dropped
On-time delivery was the only question significant in all three checks
slides.narration: The first finding was a business one: price and the app weren't what drove happiness. Delivery timing and the courier were.

slides.title: Six models that didn't make it

metrics.label: Test AUC above CV AUC by

bullets: SVM, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, CatBoost, LightGBM (Hyperopt) and an MLP neural network
Good test scores didn't hold up across cross-validation folds
The MLP collapsed and predicted every customer as unhappy
Key insight: one model with one feature set couldn't be good at both classes
slides.narration: He tried six popular models first and they all hit a ceiling. The lesson: no single model could recognise both happy and unhappy customers well.

slides.title: The insight: two moments in the journey

steps.label: Ordering
steps.detail: X3, "I ordered everything I wanted": the pre-delivery frustration signal. Random Forest uses it and becomes the unhappy specialist

steps.label: Delivery
steps.detail: X1 on time + X5 courier: the shared baseline both models use

steps.label: Doorstep
steps.detail: X2, "contents as expected": the post-delivery confirmation signal. KNN uses it and becomes the happy specialist

steps.label: Combine
steps.detail: Average both models' probabilities equally; predict happy if the result is at least 0.47

slides.narration: Here's the clever part. Unhappiness starts at ordering, and happiness is sealed at the doorstep. So he gave each moment its own model and averaged their answers.

slides.title: Results on the 26-row test set

bars.label: Best of the six earlier models

slides.narration: Together, the two models kept Random Forest's strength on unhappy customers and won back two happy ones it had missed. They made different mistakes, so combining them cancelled some out.

slides.title: Reading these numbers honestly
bullets: With 26 test rows, one customer moves recall by 7–8 points, so gaps between models are within noise
The 0.47 threshold was tuned on the same test set it's reported on, so 88.5% is optimistic
Cross-validation (above) is the more realistic estimate
Some choices were made by hand, e.g. the Random Forest features and K = 13 in the ensemble
slides.narration: He's upfront about this: the test set is tiny and the threshold was tuned on it. Cross-validation gives a more realistic, more modest picture, and he reports both.

slides.title: What the business can do with it
bullets: On-time delivery and courier quality are the foundation: low scores on both almost always mean unhappy
Unhappiness starts before delivery: "couldn't order everything I wanted" is a stock and catalogue problem, not a delivery one
Happiness is sealed at the doorstep: wrong items or substitutions break it
Price and the app aren't pain points today, but the app is worth rechecking after expansion
slides.narration: The business takeaways matter as much as the model: fix stock gaps, get orders right at the doorstep, and keep deliveries on time.

slides.title: What's next, and explore it yourself
bullets: Next: tune the threshold and features inside cross-validation, then test on new held-out data
Collect more survey responses to make the results reliable
Biggest lesson: on small data, report cross-validation alongside the test score
